beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new, just a heading. I'm wondering whether this is the IT module or the one for me.

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: nothing new. It's a brochure paragraph that could sit in any deck.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: Three reading links, one pointing at a Module 3 trigger list I'm not sure I did. I feel a bit behind already.

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (direct and indirect prompt injection, secrets in context, tool confusion, skill supply chain) and a plain access review
beats.got: The list is mostly jargon I haven't had explained. I did notice "compliant, violating and I can't tell", which is how I'd think about people rules too.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I'm asked what I'd check before this goes near real people. For me that's employee data, so the works council and the DPO come first.

beats.trigger: A tool call is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent writes a request as text and the system turns it into an action. That helps me see where a mistake could actually do something.

beats.trigger: Leading companies are investing in enablement programmes, champions networks and training, and the ones that start early will be best placed.
beats.got: nothing new. It's the usual "start early" line.

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: Old security assumed the software behaves the same every time, and agents don't. It's a clear way to say why the old checklists fall short.

beats.trigger: The dangerous move is getting your agent to *decide* to do something harmful with access it has, through well-formed English in a document it reads.
beats.got: An ordinary document can steer the agent, with no hacking involved. That is new to me and worrying, since HR files are full of free text.

beats.trigger: Remember that success with AI is everyone's responsibility.
beats.got: nothing new.

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: nothing new. This is the same paragraph I already read.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: Giving the agent less access limits how bad a mistake can get. It's a principle I can explain to my leadership team.

beats.trigger: Should the agent draft customer-facing language? If that is where the biggest risk lives, a human drafts and the agent reviews.
beats.got: The safest control is often to leave the human doing a task. That gives me a way to answer the "which roles go" question that isn't yes or no.

beats.trigger: Industry analysts expect agent adoption to accelerate significantly over the coming years.
beats.got: nothing new.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent loads when the work matches.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable checklist the agent loads when needed. I think I could hand that to an HR partner. I'm unsure about the system from modules 2-3 that it runs on.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Some rules the agent can check from files and others need a person's judgment. I'd have asked which of those need my DPO.

beats.trigger: the customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript
beats.got: I get to say what matters in my own words, and for me that's employee data and what the works council would object to. This part feels like mine.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: There are two lenses, company policy and agent risk, and the agent keeps asking me questions. It's long, but I'm following.

beats.trigger: Make the rules sound like your company's policy, not a generic GDPR template.
beats.got: I should push back when the output sounds like generic GDPR, and I know my own policies well enough to do that.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: This is the save step. The commands are for people who live in a terminal, and I'd ask someone from IT to sit next to me.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The agent checks add to our normal controls and don't replace them. That is reassuring to hear.

beats.trigger: Clear communication, strong sponsorship and regular follow-up remain the foundation, and agents are simply one more area where those principles apply.
beats.got: nothing new.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: I check that my skill shows up. It's a small step and it's fine.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit returns three lists, and some things I thought were fine come back as "I can't tell". I like that it admits uncertainty instead of giving a false green.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: The agent ranks the risks and explains each one. I'm uneasy, and the module says that unease is the point.

beats.trigger: It is important to involve the right stakeholders early, to follow best practices, and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: nothing new.

beats.trigger: The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.
beats.got: I can take the report to the DPO or the works council with a narrow, specific question. That is what I've been putting off.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent.
beats.got: We fixed one risk today, and a real agent needs all of them done. I hadn't thought about how much work is left.

beats.trigger: the ones that start early will be best placed.
beats.got: nothing new.

beats.trigger: The unease stays. Two things travel: the reusable check, and the root instructions file's rules for the risk you found.
beats.got: The agent writes what it learned into a rules file so the next session starts smarter. I can see how that carries over to a team.

beats.trigger: To share, give a teammate the skill and install it in their runtime.
beats.got: A skill can be handed to a colleague, so one person's method becomes the team's. I could do this with my HR partners, for example for a weekly people briefing.

beats.trigger: Remember that success with AI is everyone's responsibility.
beats.got: nothing new.

beats.trigger: Write one sentence per case: "the missing organisational check was X."
beats.got: There's homework: one sentence for each of two cases about the missing check. "Your call" at the end reads a little pushy.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: I read two real failures and ask what check was missing. That is a people-and-process question, and I like it.

take_homes: Give the agent less access. Not opening a door is the cheapest safety measure, and sometimes the human should keep the task.

An ordinary document can steer an agent, so anything it reads is part of the risk. The audit also says "I can't tell" honestly, and those are the items to take to a real owner such as the DPO, legal or the works council.
A skill is a reusable check I can give to my HR partners, so one person's method becomes the team's.

monday.move: Write down the people-data an agent would touch for my weekly metrics summary, then ask the DPO and the works council representative a narrow question about it before building anything.
monday.who: DPO, works council representative, and one HR partner
monday.when: Monday morning, as a short meeting request
monday.stop_condition: If the DPO says employee data can't go into this tool, I stop and don't build the metrics agent yet.
monday.blocker: I haven't asked the works council or the DPO yet, and I can't run the terminal steps without IT help.

misconception.why: The module was about safety, access and checks. It never touched which roles go or who is affected, so my headcount question is still open. The "human drafts, agent reviews" idea hints that roles get redesigned rather than just cut, but nobody said that.

one_line: The "give it less access" idea and the audit with its "I can't tell" answers were worth it, but the terminal steps are for IT people and the nine filler paragraphs made me stop reading.
